ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Bruce Lee Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Urgent follow-up four days after an emergency visit for a first convulsive collapse: history from him and a witness, triggers, examination, ECG, laboratory tests, driving and seizure safety, cannabis counseling, chronic back pain, and urgent epilepsy referral. Concerns: He wants to know what happened and whether it will happen again, and to keep training and making films; He does not want a daily medicine unless it is clearly needed, and wants to understand the evidence and decide for himself; His back pain must not stop him training. [S]

tr.td: Acetaminophen 500 mg oral tablet, one or two tablets up to three times a day when needed for back pain, no more than 3,000 mg a day
One or two tablets up to three times a day as needed; at most 3,000 mg a day
Naproxen 500 mg oral tablet, one tablet twice a day with food for seven days
One tablet twice a day with food for seven days
Twelve-lead electrocardiogram in the clinic: sinus bradycardia at 56 per minute, normal PR and QRS intervals, QTc 412 ms, no pre-excitation, Brugada pattern or signs of cardiomyopathy
Advance care planning conversation, about 15 minutes, with his consent

MRI of the brain with an epilepsy protocol (thin coronal slices through the hippocampi, FLAIR and susceptibility sequences): normal; no hippocampal sclerosis, cortical malformation, tumor, scar, old hemorrhage or swelling

Sleep-deprived electroencephalogram, about 60 minutes, with wakefulness, drowsiness and light sleep, hyperventilation and photic stimulation: normal background; no epileptiform discharges; no photoparoxysmal response
Tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap)

tr.td: Urgent follow-up four days after an emergency visit for a first convulsive collapse: history from him and a witness, triggers, examination, ECG, laboratory tests, driving and seizure safety, cannabis counseling, chronic back pain, and urgent epilepsy referral
Epilepsy clinic: MRI brain with epilepsy protocol, sleep-deprived EEG, classification, and the decision on an antiseizure medicine
One-month review: no further events, sleep and heat plan, kidney function and creatine kinase, back pain program
Two-month review: seizure-free, safety and driving, results of preventive tests, back pain and return to full training
Same-week sick visit for an acute flare of low back pain

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Culturally appropriate care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and in which language; explain the evidence plainly and let him decide; respect his own training methods and philosophy; share information with his family only as he chooses
Urgent referral to the epilepsy clinic within the week, with MRI of the brain with an epilepsy protocol and a sleep-deprived EEG
Laboratory tests after the seizure: sodium, glucose, calcium, magnesium, kidney function, creatine kinase, blood count and TSH, with creatine kinase and creatinine repeated until normal

No driving until the epilepsy clinic has seen him and the period without seizures it advises has passed; Hong Kong's driving licence regulations list epilepsy and liability to sudden fainting among the conditions for which the Commissioner for Transport must refuse or cancel a licence

Seizure safety: no swimming alone, no work at heights or with dangerous machinery, showers rather than baths, and seizure first aid taught to the people he works with; a stunt double for falls and heights until the clinic advises otherwise

Triggers: at least seven hours of sleep, regular meals, breaks and air conditioning during long recording and training sessions, and drinking to thirst with salty food or an electrolyte drink in the heat rather than large volumes of plain water
Cannabis: a nonjudgmental conversation about cannabis, heat, sleep loss and seizures; he chose to stop while his risk is highest; no synthetic cannabinoids

Medicine safety: avoid medicines that lower the seizure threshold, such as tramadol, bupropion and high doses of sedating antihistamines, and sedatives whose withdrawal can provoke seizures, such as meprobamate and carisoprodol; tell any doctor or pharmacist about the seizure

Chronic back pain: a structured core strengthening and motor control program with a physical therapist, heat, and acetaminophen when needed; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only in short courses, with food and normal fluids; no opioids

No antiseizure medicine after this first unprovoked seizure, by shared decision: his two-year recurrence risk is at the lower end of 21% to 45% with a normal MRI and EEG; immediate treatment would lower the two-year risk but not change long-term remission; a second unprovoked seizure would mean epilepsy and starting a medicine such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine
None in the two months since the first
Sleep at least seven hours a night, including on film schedules
About seven hours a night from the first month
No cannabis while the seizure risk is highest
None since the seizure, by his report
Back pain at 3 or less out of 10 with full training
Pain 2 out of 10 after a flare that settled within a week
